11633-parsifal-a-mystical-drama-by-richa:
Oliver Huckel retells Wagner's Parsifal in the spirit of the Bayreuth interpretation, in three parts: the coming of Parsifal, the tempting of Parsifal, and the crowning of Parsifal. A castle rises in mountain woods above a smiling lake, home of the knights of the Holy Grail.

Kundry laughs and groans, Klingsor speaks of wounded knights, and a youth stands proud on garden walls, roses laughing in his cheeks. The retelling, published by Crowell, keeps Wagner's music drama in English verse and prose, with pictures of Monsalvat, the Grail communion, and Parsifal healing Amfortas.
1713-lincoln-an-account-of-his-personal-:
Nathaniel Wright Stephenson writes a life of Abraham Lincoln that stays close to the man rather than the monument. It traces his youth in Illinois, his law practice, and his marriage before the presidency. Notes and a bibliography back the main claims, and disputed points are argued in the notes instead of smoothed over.

The heart of the book is Lincoln under the strain of the Civil War: his melancholy, his belief in dreams and signs, and the way responsibility deepened rather than hardened him. Readers looking for Lincoln's character — patient, superstitious in his own way, and haunted by the war's cost — will find it in letters and the testimony of those near him.
24926-in-the-mahdi-s-grasp:
George Manville Fenn wrote In the Mahdi's Grasp about a young army officer held as a slave in the Sudan, long thought dead. His friends in London, one a skilled surgeon, sail to Cairo and push south, winning trust by cures and winning the ear of an influential sheikh. Their goal is the missing Harry, held in the Mahdi's stronghold.

Harry breaks his own arm so he can be brought to the surgeon, the Hakim, for treatment, and the party at last escapes with him straight through a battle. Their manservant, stained dark in disguise, nearly dies on the field. Fenn keeps the tension high through a long, informative tale of rescue in the Sudan wars.
27571-christianity-and-greek-philosophy-:
B. F. Cocker, professor of moral and mental philosophy at the University of Michigan, published this study in New York, San Francisco, and Cincinnati in 1870. Its full title states its theme: the relation between spontaneous and reflective thought in Greece and the positive teaching of Christ and his apostles.

Cocker takes Augustine's saying as epigraph: Plato revealed the true God, while Christ showed the way to him. He writes to deepen faith by showing that Christian truth rests not solely on special facts, but on all the facts of nature and humanity. The volume joins Greek philosophy and Christian teaching in one argument.

lincoln-an-account-of-his-personal-life-:
Nathaniel Wright Stephenson studies Lincoln's own life in this book. His subtitle stresses the springs of Lincoln's acts. The ordeal of war revealed and deepened those springs, he argues. Stephenson thanks William Roscoe Thayer for John Hay's manuscript diary.

Helen Nicolay confirmed points from the official life for him. Lincoln's last living secretary, Colonel Stoddard, gave kind aid. Henry Johnson found Lincoln's work as a lawyer in a slave case. Judge Marshall checked and filled out that curious case for the book. A futile search for Republican committee papers also aided his certainty. Professor Ulrich Phillips helped the Chandler inquiries generously. Plain talk and close facts mark Stephenson's approach to his subject throughout.
nasa-tm-19660014179-scientific-basis-of-:
Alexander G Smith of the University of Florida gave this address in January 1966 on observing the universe from space, issued as a Marshall memorandum on March 24, 1966. His subtitle names applications of orbiting platforms and space probes in radio astronomy. Jupiter is named in the catalog note as a source of data for such work. From orbit, instruments escape the limits of Earth's air.

Smith lays out the scientific basis for that move. Radio waves from planets and stars carry facts no other signal can give. Probes can also go to the source, rather than wait for its signals. The address captures the case for space astronomy just as its first great observatories were being planned.
nasa-tm-19690008665-diurnal-and-seasonal:
H. C. Brinton, R. A. Pickett, and H. A. Taylor Jr. of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this October 1968 preprint, X-621-68-375. They report daily and seasonal changes in the ion mix of the topside ionosphere, measured by an ion mass spectrometer aboard Explorer 32. The satellite sampled the charged layer from low heights to far above Earth.

The team found ion patterns tied directly to the Sun's angle in the sky. At one northern height, oxygen ions rose sharply at dawn and ruled the daytime layer. Hydrogen ions ruled at night instead, far stronger than by day. Seasonal contrasts between summer and winter hemispheres showed in the oxygen and nitrogen patterns. Hydrogen and helium changed far less across the seasons.
